hazards.bypass-controller: You jumpered the controller to force the pump on. The controller is the listed device that starts, runs and protects the pump; jumpered, it has no overload, no phase protection and no record of the run.
hazards.flow-indoors: You opened the test header with the discharge pointed into the pump room. Two thousand gallons a minute at 100 psi fills the room, floods the controller and knocks a person off their feet; the hose lines go to the outside discharge.
hazards.no-notify-run: You started the pump without notifying the alarm company. A fire pump running trips the waterflow and pump-running signals — the fire department rolls to a building with no fire, and the next real signal from this building gets a slower response.
hazards.suction-closed: You started the pump with the suction control valve closed. A centrifugal pump with no water at the suction cavitates and destroys its impeller and seal in minutes — the suction gauge is read before the pump is called.

interrupts.alert: The alarm panel is reporting a hot work permit opened on the third floor. The sprinkler system is still impaired for your test.
interrupts.cue: Nobody strikes an arc in a building with the pump on test.
interrupts.missNote: You ran the test to completion with hot work live in an unprotected building. Impairment plus ignition source is the specific sequence behind most total-loss fires in sprinklered buildings, and it is always two teams who each thought the other knew.
interrupts.why: An impairment is a window during which the building has no fire protection, and the only thing managing that window is the person on the phone to the monitoring company and the permit desk. Hot work inside it is the one combination that has burned buildings down.
interrupts.wrongNote: Get on the phone. The impairment is the emergency, not the pump reading.

interrupts.alert: The packing gland has opened up. It has gone from a drip to a stream and the floor drain is not keeping up.
interrupts.cue: Look at the gland before the room floods.
interrupts.missNote: You ran the pump at rated flow with the gland streaming. The sleeve scored, the room took an inch of water, and the pump that is supposed to protect the building is now the thing that is out of service.
interrupts.why: Packing is meant to weep — a stream is not weeping, it is a gland that has backed off under vibration, and it will take the shaft sleeve with it if it runs like that at flow.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the gland. Nothing about the flow test is worth a wrecked shaft sleeve and a flooded pump room.

lateNotes.controller-start: The alarm company is told, the discharge is laid and the suction is proven before the pump is called.
lateNotes.restore-auto: The test points are done and the header closed before the controller goes back to automatic.

name: Fire Pump

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the pump's rated flow and pressure, last year's test points, and the test-header size.
steps.prompt: Check the pump's rated flow and pressure, last year's test points, and the test-header size.
steps.title: Read the test record and the nameplate curve
steps.why: The nameplate states what the pump is rated to deliver — flow, pressure, rpm — and last year's NFPA 25 test record states what it actually delivered a year ago. This year's churn, 100% and 150% readings are judged against both curves, because a pump that still meets its nameplate but has drifted from last year's numbers is already telling you something is wearing.

steps.cue: Call the monitoring company to put the account on test, and tell building management.
steps.prompt: Call the monitoring company to put the account on test, and tell building management.
steps.title: Notify the alarm company and the building
steps.why: Running the pump sends a pump-running signal to the monitoring company exactly the way a real fire would, and an un-notified signal gets a fire department dispatched to a building with nothing burning. Putting the account on test before the pump turns holds that dispatch for the window, and calling back afterward takes the building off test before the next real signal needs to be believed.

steps.cue: Read the suction gauge with the supply control valve open and commit inside the positive band.

gauge.label: SUCTION
gauge.missNote: Suction not in the band — check the supply control valve before calling the pump.

steps.prompt: Read the suction gauge with the supply control valve open and commit inside the positive band.
steps.title: Confirm suction and the supply valve open
steps.why: A centrifugal fire pump needs a positive column of water at its suction before it is ever called to run; a closed control valve or a dropped municipal supply starves the impeller of the water it needs to cool and lubricate itself. That shows up on this gauge first — read before the pump is started, not after the bearings have already cooked.

steps.cue: Hose lines off the test header, run outside to a safe discharge, playpipes secured for the pitot readings.

itemNames.hose-lay: hose lines from the test header

steps.outOfOrderNote: Lay the lines, run them outside, then secure the nozzles — in that order.
steps.prompt: Hose lines off the test header, run outside to a safe discharge, playpipes secured for the pitot readings.
steps.title: Lay the test hoses to a safe discharge
steps.why: The test flows the pump's full rated capacity — a thousand gallons a minute or more — and where that water goes has to be decided before the header valve opens, not while it is running. Lines laid outside to a discharge that can actually take it, playpipes secured so the pitot readings hold steady, keep that flow from finding the nearest person or the pump room floor instead.

steps.cue: Turn the controller selector from automatic to manual for the test.
steps.prompt: Turn the controller selector from automatic to manual for the test.
steps.title: Controller to manual test
steps.why: In manual, the pump starts and stops on your command alone. Left in automatic during the test, a pressure drop anywhere on the system — even one your own hoses cause — starts the pump before you are positioned to read it, and the controller's own timer can stop it again mid-reading and void the point.

steps.cue: Start the pump with the test header closed and read the churn pressure.
steps.prompt: Start the pump with the test header closed and read the churn pressure.
steps.title: Start the pump at churn
steps.why: Churn — the no-flow point — is the first reading on the curve, and it also proves the motor starts, comes up to rated speed and holds steady discharge pressure before a gallon of water moves. A large fire-pump motor coming up to speed is loud enough to trigger OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.95 hearing-conservation threshold, so hearing protection goes on with the start command, not after the noise surprises you.

steps.cue: Read the discharge gauge at churn and commit inside the nameplate band.

gauge.label: CHURN
gauge.missNote: Churn pressure off the nameplate — record it and investigate before flowing.

steps.prompt: Read the discharge gauge at churn and commit inside the nameplate band.
steps.title: Read the churn pressure
steps.why: Churn pressure sitting above the nameplate band means the relief valve is holding it there correctly; well below it points to a worn impeller, a slipping coupling or the pump running at the wrong speed. It is the first number written on the test sheet, and every reading after it is judged against this one.

steps.cue: Open the test header valves until the pitot readings total rated flow, and commit the discharge pressure.

gauge.label: 100% FLOW
gauge.missNote: Not at rated flow — adjust the header valves and read the pitots again.

steps.prompt: Open the test header valves until the pitot readings total rated flow, and commit the discharge pressure.
steps.title: Open the header to 100% flow
steps.why: Rated flow at rated pressure is the exact point stamped on the pump's nameplate, and hitting it is the one reading that says this pump can still deliver what the building's sprinkler design assumed it could. Miss it low and every sprinkler head downstream of this pump is protected by less water than the design called for.

steps.cue: Open to 150% of rated flow and hold while the pressure, current and speed are read.
steps.holdBreakNote: Flow dropped before the readings were done — reopen and hold the 150% point.
steps.prompt: Open to 150% of rated flow and hold while the pressure, current and speed are read.
steps.title: Hold the 150% flow point
steps.why: At 150% of rated flow, NFPA 25 requires the pump still make at least 65% of its rated pressure — the point where a worn impeller or a slipping motor shows up hardest. Current, speed and pressure are all read with the flow held steady at that point, not caught on the way past it while the needle is still moving.

steps.cue: Motor amps on each phase and pump rpm with the tachometer, recorded against each flow point.
steps.prompt: Motor amps on each phase and pump rpm with the tachometer, recorded against each flow point.
steps.title: Read current and speed
steps.why: Pressure alone can hide a motor slipping under load or a pump running slower than its rated speed while still making a pressure that looks acceptable on the gauge. Motor current on each phase and pump rpm from the tachometer are what tie that pressure back to the curve and catch a fault the discharge gauge alone would miss.

steps.cue: Header closed, pump stopped, selector to automatic, supply valve confirmed open, alarm company off test.
steps.prompt: Header closed, pump stopped, selector to automatic, supply valve confirmed open, alarm company off test.
steps.title: Close the header, controller to automatic, call the alarm company back
steps.why: A fire pump left in manual mode will not start itself for a real fire — it will sit at the panel waiting for a hand that is not there. Closing the header, confirming the supply valve open, returning the selector to automatic and calling the alarm company off test is the last sequence of the job, and the one that actually returns the building's protection.

steps.cue: Inspect the pump, driver, controller and valves after the test and click the defect.

itemNotes.packing-leak: The packing gland is running dry and hot — no drip. Packing needs a steady drip to cool it; dry, it scores the shaft. Adjusted and written up before the room is locked.

steps.prompt: Inspect the pump, driver, controller and valves after the test and click the defect.
steps.title: Walk the pump room before locking up
steps.why: Running the pump at full flow heats bearings, stresses the packing and shakes loose whatever the room was hiding while it sat idle for a year. The walk-through right after, while everything is still warm and still moving, is where a gland running dry gets caught and adjusted, not left to score a shaft sleeve before next year's test finds it.
